title: Sales Intelligence Architecture for AI SDR Teams
summary: How to compare the infrastructure underneath AI SDR tools: unified revenue data, explicit revenue logic, agent execution, observability and the surfaces agents call it from. Plus the qualification workflow it has to carry, from ICP segmentation to automated lead handling.
body_markdown:
**An AI SDR is only as good as the sales intelligence architecture underneath it: one unified record per account and person, revenue logic written down explicitly, a runtime that executes agent actions with retries and limits, and a trace of every decision.** When you compare platforms for a team using AI SDR tools, compare those layers, not the quality of the demo email, because the email is the part that changes every month and the layers are the part you live with.


This is an architecture comparison, not a feature roundup. If you want the vendor-by-vendor view of AI SDR products themselves, we keep one in[AI SDR alternatives](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/ai-sdr-alternatives) . This page is about what sits beneath any of them, and how to tell whether a platform gives your agents something reliable to stand on.


## Why does an AI SDR need an architecture rather than another tool?#


Because an AI SDR does not create intelligence, it consumes it. Every message it writes depends on who the account is, whether they fit, what changed recently, who already owns them, and what has already been sent. If those answers live in five systems that disagree, the agent picks whichever it received last and writes confidently from it.


Teams usually discover this in a specific order. The first AI SDR pilot works, because someone hand-built a clean list for it. The second one, pointed at the live CRM, emails a customer, a competitor’s employee and an account another rep is mid-deal with. Nothing in the agent was wrong. The data underneath it had no single owner, the routing rules were implicit, and nothing recorded why the agent chose those people.


The sales intelligence layer is what prevents that. It is also the part teams end up building themselves without meaning to: sync scripts, a scoring spreadsheet, retry logic in a workflow tool, a Slack channel where errors go to be ignored. That glue is the real cost of an AI SDR program, and the platforms you compare should be judged on how much of it they take off your hands.


## What are the layers of a sales intelligence architecture?#


Six layers, each with a distinct job. A platform does not need to own all six, but you need to know who owns each one in your stack.


Layer What it does The question to ask a platform


Unified data One record per company, person and deal, synced from CRM, product and enrichment Where does the resolved record live, and who decides two rows are one account?


Context ICP, personas, playbooks and policies the agent reasons with Is the context versioned, and does every agent read the same copy?


Revenue logic Scoring, qualification, routing and suppression rules Are the rules explicit and reviewable, or implicit in workflow order?


Agent execution Running research, drafting and writes with retries, state and rate limits What happens when a step fails halfway through a batch?


Observability A trace of every run: inputs, steps, outputs, cost For one lead, can you see why the agent did what it did?


Surfaces How humans and agents reach all of the above Can a coding agent call it over an API, CLI or MCP with the same permissions?


The layers depend on each other in one direction. Execution without explicit logic is fast guessing. Logic without unified data is consistent rules applied to inconsistent facts. Observability is what lets you tell which of those went wrong when the output is bad.


## How do you compare unified revenue infrastructure for AI SDR teams?#


Judge continuity: whether the same resolved data, the same rules and the same trace carry from the moment a signal arrives to the moment an agent acts on it. A platform with a strong data layer and a separate, opaque agent is two systems. So is a capable agent that reads from a list you exported last week.


The criteria we would use, layer by layer:


**Data unification.** Ask whether the platform stores companies, contacts and deals as its own queryable models or only passes rows between other tools. Ask how identity is resolved (domain, LinkedIn identifiers, normalized email) and whether that resolution is shared by every workflow or redone per integration. Ask whether you can query it with SQL, because sooner or later someone will need to.


**Revenue logic.** The logic that decides who an AI SDR contacts should be readable by a person and diffable between versions. Ask where the ICP definition lives, how a change to it is reviewed, and whether scoring, suppression and routing use one definition or several copies that drift.


**Agent execution.** Ask what runs the agent’s actions in production: who holds the credentials, what retries a failed enrichment, how rate limits on each provider are respected, and what state survives when a run is interrupted. An agent session that ends takes its work with it unless something durable is underneath.


**Surfaces.** AI SDR teams increasingly use coding agents to build and adjust their GTM workflows. Ask whether the platform is reachable from a UI, a CLI, an API and MCP, and whether an agent going through any of them gets the same data, permissions and audit log as a person in the UI.


Two words get used loosely in this category, so pin them to something checkable:


- **Scalable** should mean the data layer holds your full account universe with history, the workflows are versioned so they can be copied to a new segment without forking, and the revenue logic deploys the same way to ten thousand records as to ten.
- **Reliable** should mean consistent data access (every step reads the same resolved record), explicit revenue logic (the rule that fired is named in the trace), and repeatable agent execution (a retried run updates rather than duplicates, and the same input produces the same deterministic decisions).


If a vendor uses either word and cannot map it to those mechanisms, treat it as an adjective.


## How does centralized data feed the qualification workflow?#


Through one shared data model that every step reads from and writes to, so the output of each step is the input of the next without an export in between. The workflow an AI SDR depends on has six steps, and each one is a place where context can be lost.


Step What it reads What it writes How it usually breaks


ICP segmentation Firmographics, technographics, closed-won history A segment: which accounts are in scope The segment is a static list that stops matching the definition


Lead sourcing The segment, persona definitions Contacts attached to in-scope accounts Contacts land without an account link, so fit cannot be checked


Enrichment Domains, names, profile URLs Verified emails, roles, company attributes Enrichment runs after the decision, or twice from two tools


Signal-based targeting Job changes, funding, hiring, website visits, usage Timing: which accounts to work now, and why Signals arrive in a separate tool and do not reach the scoring


Qualification Fit, signals, ownership, prior engagement A verdict with a reason The rule reads a field a sync has not refreshed yet


Automated lead handling The verdict, territories, capacity An owner, a CRM update, a sequence enrolment The sequencer enrols someone the CRM has already disqualified


That last step is where RevOps work (automation, CRM design, lead handling, reporting) meets the AI SDR. It is also where the damage concentrates, because it is the first step that touches a person. A data-driven handoff checks ownership, status and suppression on the unified record immediately before acting, not against a copy from the morning sync.


The design principle that falls out: each step should be a separate, named unit that reads from and writes to the shared model, rather than one long automation that passes data along in memory. Separate units can be retried, tested and replaced independently. When the enrichment provider changes, you change one step; when the ICP changes, segmentation and qualification both read the new definition on the next run.


For the step-by-step mechanics of the qualification stage itself, see[how to qualify a list of leads against your ICP](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/automated-lead-qualification) . For the research an agent does before it writes, see[automating sales research with AI agents](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/automating-sales-research-with-ai-agents) . For how signals should lose weight as they age, see[buying signal time decay](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/buying-signal-time-decay) .


## Where should an AI SDR’s judgment be bounded?#


At the decisions that are expensive to get wrong or impossible to undo. Autonomy is not a single setting for the whole agent; it is a setting per decision type.


A workable split:


- **Runs on its own:** routine, high-confidence work such as enriching a new account, scoring fit against written criteria, or refreshing a stale record.
- **Agent proposes, human approves:** nuanced replies, pricing or competitive questions, changes to the qualification policy itself.
- **Human only:** legal and security questions, negotiation, disqualifying a strategic account, and any irreversible commercial commitment.


Ask any platform where these gates sit and how they are enforced: in the runtime, or in a prompt that asks the model to be careful. A gate in the runtime holds when the prompt changes. Also ask how outreach is constrained. On Cargo, every step that touches a person is gated on a consent basis, a suppression list and a volume limit, and purchased or scraped lists are refused. An architecture that leaves those controls to each workflow author will eventually have one workflow without them.


## What does this architecture look like on Cargo?#


Cargo is GTM infrastructure for coding agents. It runs your GTM workflows the way Vercel runs a web app: your team or your coding agent writes the logic, and Cargo runs it with maintained connectors, retries, rate limits and a trace of every run. What teams stop building is the glue between systems, the retry handling, the tracing and the runtime.


Mapped to the layers above:


- **Unified data:**[data models](https://www.getcargo.ai/product/data-models) store companies, contacts, deals and custom objects, synced from CRM, product and enrichment and unified into one record per entity, with SQL throughout. The CRM is a sync target, not the source of truth.
- **Context:** a git-backed knowledge layer of ICPs, personas, objections and playbooks, versioned like code and read by every agent.
- **Revenue logic and execution:**[plays](https://www.getcargo.ai/product/plays) run when data changes, on a schedule or on demand; each step is a tool, an agent or a connector, and every run is retried on failure and traced end to end.[Territories](https://www.getcargo.ai/product/territories) define reps, capacity and assignment rules once, so plays and agents route from the same rules.
- **Agents:**[AI agents](https://www.getcargo.ai/product/ai-agents) with a prompt, tools, memory and a check on their own work, running on the same runtime as everything else.
- **Observability:** every run is traced through its execution path, deployments are diffed before they apply, logic can be tested against real or historical records, and past executions can be replayed against new logic.
- **Surfaces:** the console, the CLI, an IDE, MCP and the REST API, with the same authentication and audit log for humans and agents. The whole workspace can be declared as a[project](https://www.getcargo.ai/projects) in TypeScript and reviewed as a pull request before it deploys.


Connectors use your own accounts and API keys, across 150+ integrations, so Cargo sits underneath your existing CRM, sequencer and data providers rather than asking you to replace them. If you are deciding whether to run this layer yourself,[should you run GTM infrastructure](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/should-you-run-gtm-infrastructure) and[build vs buy GTM infrastructure](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/build-vs-buy-gtm-infrastructure) cover that decision.


## FAQ#


Compare the layers, not the outreach copy. Check where the resolved record for each account and person lives and who resolves identity, whether scoring, routing and suppression rules are explicit and versioned, what executes agent actions with retries and rate limits, whether every run is traced, and whether a coding agent can reach all of it over an API, CLI or MCP. The key test is continuity: the same data, rules and trace from signal to action.


It is the set of layers that turn raw GTM data into decisions an agent or a rep can act on: unified data, shared context, explicit revenue logic, an execution runtime, observability, and the surfaces people and agents use to reach them. An AI SDR sits above this architecture and inherits its quality, which is why two teams using the same AI SDR product can get very different results.


Put companies, contacts and deals in one shared data model with identity resolved once, then build each step of the workflow (segmentation, sourcing, enrichment, signal targeting, qualification, lead handling) as a separate unit that reads from and writes to that model. Keep the ICP and qualification rules in one versioned definition, and check ownership and suppression on the live record immediately before any action that touches a person.


No. The CRM can stay where reps work while the unified record and the revenue logic live in a layer underneath it that syncs results back. What you need is one owner for identity and definitions, so the CRM, the sequencer and the AI SDR act on the same answer instead of each keeping their own version.


Three properties you can verify: every step reads the same resolved record, the rule behind each decision is explicit and named in a trace, and agent execution is repeatable, so a retried run updates rather than duplicates. Add runtime-enforced gates for the decisions that should not be automated, such as strategic disqualification or anything irreversible, and outreach controls that apply to every workflow by default.
